input:
When a pump draws liquid from an open tank, it is essential to verify that the suction conditions are adequate, and this is done by calculating the available net positive suction head, commonly denoted $NPSH_a$, at the pump inlet. The calculation brings together several quantities: the pressure acting on the liquid surface in the tank, $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure of the liquid, $P_v$, at the pumping temperature, the liquid density $\rho$, the gravitational acceleration $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$ between the liquid surface and the pump, and the friction loss $h_f$ in the suction line, combined in the following relationship:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In essence, the first term of the expression converts the margin of pressure above the vapour pressure into an equivalent head of the liquid itself, while the lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are effectively consumed before the liquid reaches the inlet. In the present case, the tank is open to the atmosphere, so $P_{atm}$ corresponds to the atmospheric pressure of 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, which means that the pressure margin available above the vapour pressure is 81.4 kPa. The static lift amounts to 1.6 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 0.4 m. Taking all of these values together, the available net positive suction head works out at 6.3 m. It is instructive to note that the pressure term on its own contributes 8.3 m of head, while the lift and the friction losses together remove 2.0 m. This matters because, if the available head were to fall to the level the pump requires, the pressure at the inlet would reach the vapour pressure and cavitation would occur, so the margin between the two values provides valuable protection. The required net positive suction head at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value of 6.3 m must exceed it with an adequate margin. As the required value is not stated here, the comparison against the vendor curve remains the outstanding check, highlighting the importance of confirming the margin before the installation is finalised.
target:
A pump draws light oil from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head at the pump inlet is to be determined from the suction conditions. The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ (m) is calculated from the pressure at the liquid surface in the tank $P_{atm}$ (kPa), the vapour pressure of the oil $P_v$ (kPa) at the pumping temperature, the oil density $\rho$ (kg m⁻³), the gravitational acceleration $g$ (m s⁻²), the static lift $h_{lift}$ (m) between the liquid surface and the pump inlet, and the friction loss $h_f$ (m) in the suction line:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The first term converts the pressure margin above the vapour pressure into a head of the oil itself; the lift and the friction loss are then subtracted, because both are spent before the oil reaches the inlet. The tank is open to the atmosphere, so $P_{atm}$ is the atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, and the pressure margin above it is thus 81.4 kPa. The static lift is 1.6 m and the suction-line friction loss is 0.4 m. For the stated conditions the available net positive suction head is 6.3 m. The pressure term contributes 8.3 m of that head, and the lift and friction together remove 2.0 m. Where the available head falls to the head the pump requires, the pressure at the inlet reaches the vapour pressure and the pump cavitates; the margin between the two values is the protection against that condition. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow is read from the vendor curve, and the available value of 6.3 m must exceed it with margin. The required value is not stated here, so the comparison with the vendor curve is the check that remains: the available head is fixed by the suction conditions stated above, and it is the required head from the curve that decides whether the margin is adequate.
